title: Z-K-R
hook: zachor, zikaron: memory as something you do

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-M-A: hear, understand, obey, one root. Your line was to hear is to heed. Did you listen to the end of one conversation? Today closes the week, with the root of remembering. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

"And God remembered Noah." The water still covers everything. The ark is drifting. Nothing in the story has moved for a long time. Then comes that sentence, and right after it, God sends a wind across the earth, and the waters begin to go down. Read it slowly and something stands out. Remembering here isn't a thought drifting through a mind. It's the hinge. It's the moment things start to move again. Today's root is memory that does something.
screen: `AND GOD REMEMBERED NOAH.` → `A WIND, AND THE WATERS GO DOWN.` → `MEMORY AS A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Z-K-R. Zayin, kaf, resh. Four places it shows up. First, when God remembers. Noah is one. In Exodus, the people groan under slavery, and the text says "God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob." A few verses on, Moses is standing at a burning bush. Memory, again, is where rescue starts. Second, zachor, remember, as a command. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The commandment isn't asking anyone to recall that the Sabbath exists. Remembering it means keeping it: lighting candles, setting a table, a day set apart. Third, zikaron, a memorial. Of the Passover night, the Torah says: "And this day shall be unto you for a memorial." And the seder is remembering done with your hands and mouth: matzah to chew, bitter herbs to taste, questions asked out loud. Fourth, people. When a Jew mentions someone who has died, it's customary to add zichrono livracha, may his memory be a blessing. The memory is given a job. And since today ends a week, remember what this week's roots held. K-D-Sh, set apart. Tz-D-K, giving as justice. Ch-S-D, kindness. A-M-N, steadiness. Emet, truth with its first letter. Sh-M-A, hearing that heeds. And now Z-K-R. Read closely, each of them turns out to be a thing you do.
screen: `WHEN GOD REMEMBERS, THINGS MOVE.` · `REMEMBER THE SABBATH: KEEP IT.` · `A MEMORIAL YOU CAN TASTE.` · `MAY THEIR MEMORY BE A BLESSING.` · then, large: `MEMORY IS DOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone aloud. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who isn't in your life the way they once were. Someone who has died, or someone far away. Say their name out loud, quietly. Then say one thing they did. Not a feeling about them: a thing they did, with their hands or their words. Let that sit for a few breaths. If the person has died, you can add zichrono livracha, or zichronah livracha for a woman: may their memory be a blessing. Then just breathe with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
screen: `SAY THEIR NAME.` · `SAY ONE THING THEY DID.`

segments.voice: Z-K-R. Zayin, kaf, resh: zachor, remember, and zikaron, a memorial. Memory that moves things. Today's word.
Your line: memory is doing. Today, turn one memory into one act: cook their recipe, use their phrase, call the person who knew them too. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Jews remember through acts: keeping the Sabbath, eating the foods of the Passover seder, lighting a memorial candle on the anniversary of a death, and adding 'may their memory be a blessing' after a name.

what a scholar hears: Exodus 20 says zachor, remember, and Deuteronomy 5 says shamor, keep, for the same commandment; zikaron names the Passover a memorial.
